Proskuneo
pros-koo-NEH-oh
v. (Greek)
Greek proskuneō, “to bow down, do obeisance, worship,” from pros- (toward) + kuneō (to kiss); the etymology suggests the gesture of kissing-toward (the hand or feet of) the one honored, as in the ancient practice of prostrate reverence before kings and deities.

Biblical Definition

Proskuneō is the New Testament’s great verb for worship—and the etymology is theologically pointed. The word is built from pros- (toward) + kuneō (to kiss), suggesting the literal gesture of bowing-and-kissing-toward, the prostrate physical reverence with which subjects of the ancient world honored kings and deities. The verb is therefore embodied, not merely mental or affective: proskuneō is the bowing-down before, the prostrating-oneself toward, the embodied act of homage that confesses with the body what the heart acknowledges—that the One worshipped is supremely worthy. The supreme biblical application is to God Himself. The First Commandment grounds it: Thou shalt have no other gods before me; the worship that the verb names is to be given to God alone. Christ’s answer to Satan’s third temptation makes the doctrine explicit: then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship (proskunēseis) the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve (Matt 4:10, quoting Deut 6:13). The exclusivity of true worship is not a sectarian preference; it is the divinely-grounded standard, and Christ Himself sets it. The biblical doctrine therefore has its strict positive and its strict negative. Positive: worship is to be rendered to God, freely, fully, with the whole self including the body. The Samaritan woman’s encounter with Christ at the well draws out the further specification: but the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24). True worship is therefore embodied (involving the body, the bowing, the gesture, the voice) and yet also spiritual (engaging the inner spirit, not mere outward form) and according to truth (according to the truth God has revealed of Himself, not invented by the worshipper). Negative: worship is not to be rendered to creatures. Cornelius bowing to Peter is corrected: and as Peter was coming in, Cornelius met him, and fell down at his feet, and worshipped him. But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man (Acts 10:25-26). John bowing to the angel in Revelation is twice corrected: and I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant... worship God (Rev 19:10; 22:8-9). The exclusivity is firm: no apostle, no angel, no saint, no created being is to receive the worship that belongs to God alone. The supreme Christological inference is therefore unmistakable. Christ Himself receives worship: at His birth (Matt 2:11, the wise men); during His ministry (Matt 9:18 the ruler; Matt 14:33 the disciples after the storm; Matt 15:25 the Syro-Phoenician woman; Matt 28:9 the women after the resurrection); after His resurrection (Matt 28:17 the disciples); in heaven (Heb 1:6 the angels at the Father’s command; Rev 5:14 the elders and living creatures). And He does not refuse it. If worship God alone is the standard and Christ accepts proskuneō from human and angelic worshippers, then Christ is God: the inference the NT writers draw, and the inference that grounds the Trinitarian worship of the church across every century.

Webster 1828 Definition

(Greek term.) Proskuneō: to worship, bow down, do obeisance; literally to kiss toward; the great NT verb for the embodied homage rendered to God alone (per the First Commandment and Christ’s Matt 4:10), refused by apostles and angels, received by Christ as evidence of His deity.

WORSHIP, v.t. — 1. To adore; to pay divine honors to; to reverence with supreme respect and veneration. 2. To respect; to honor; to treat with civil reverence (in lesser social usage). In scripture, the homage rendered to God alone (Matt 4:10), refused by apostles (Acts 10:25-26) and angels (Rev 19:10; 22:8-9), and received by Christ as evidence of His deity.

PROSKUNEO — (Greek verb, G4352.) To worship, bow down, do obeisance; 60 NT uses. The chief NT worship-verb.

Key Scripture

Matthew 4:10 — "Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve."

John 4:23-24 — "But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

Matthew 28:9 — "And as they went to tell his disciples, behold, Jesus met them, saying, All hail. And they came and held him by the feet, and worshipped him."

Revelation 22:8-9 — "And I John saw these things, and heard them. And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things. Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant... worship God."

Modern Corruption

Proskuneō-shaped worship is corrupted, on one side, by the disembodied register of much contemporary Western worship that has reduced the bodily homage of proskuneō to a primarily intellectual or affective inward act with little bodily expression—and on the other by the idolatrous direction of worship toward creatures (saints, angels, images, the Mary of Marian devotion, the man-centered worship of celebrity culture), against the First Commandment and Christ’s explicit Matt 4:10 standard.

expand to see more

The disembodied register of much contemporary Western worship has reduced proskuneō to a primarily intellectual or affective inward act with little bodily expression. The Greek verb is bodily: to bow down, to kiss toward, to prostrate. The biblical pattern is bodily: lifted hands (Ps 28:2; 63:4; 134:2; 1 Tim 2:8), bowed heads (Gen 24:26; Ex 34:8), bent knees (1 Kgs 8:54; Eph 3:14; Phil 2:10), prostrate bodies (Ezek 1:28; 3:23; 11:13; Matt 17:6; Rev 1:17). The disembodied contemporary register—hands in pockets, eyes on the screen, body still and uninvolved—has lost something the Greek verb physically names. The recovery is not the manufactured embodiment of stage-managed performance but the natural recovery of the body’s involvement in worship as the soul engages God: lifted hands when the heart is moved to lift, bowed head when the soul is moved to bow, kneeling when the moment calls for kneeling. The same verb the NT uses for the worship Christ accepts is the verb that has the body in it; the recovery is the recovery of the body’s involvement in the worship the Bible names.

The opposite corruption is the idolatrous direction of worship toward creatures, against the First Commandment and Christ’s Matt 4:10 standard. Various traditions have done this in various ways: Marian devotion that addresses to Mary the proskuneō Christ’s teaching reserved for God alone; the veneration of saints that escalates from honor into worship; the use of images that, however its defenders distinguish ‘veneration’ from ‘adoration,’ visually directs the worshipper’s posture toward the image rather than toward God; the celebrity-pastor culture of contemporary Western evangelicalism that, however unintentionally, trains the affections toward men rather than toward Christ; the entertainment-shaped worship that orients the gathering around what moves the worshipper rather than around the God who is worshipped. The biblical refusal is sharp and uniform: Peter refuses Cornelius’s proskuneō, the angel refuses John’s, Christ accepts proskuneō from all who offer it because He is God and the worship belongs to Him. The recovery is the strict First-Commandment-grounded exclusivity of true worship: to God alone, in spirit and in truth, with the body and the soul engaged, after the pattern the New Testament uniformly assumes and that Christ Himself sets at the climax of His wilderness temptations.

Hebrew Roots

Greek proskuneō (to worship, bow down, do obeisance), from pros- + kuneō (to kiss toward)—the great NT verb for the embodied homage rendered to God alone, refused by apostles and angels, received by Christ as evidence of His deity, and to be offered in spirit and in truth per John 4:24.

expand to see more

Greek proskuneō (G4352) — to worship, bow down (60 NT uses).

Greek latreuō (G3000) — to serve, render religious service (the cousin worship-verb; Matt 4:10 pairs the two).

Greek sebomai (G4576) — to revere, worship (Matt 15:9; Acts 16:14; 18:7).

Hebrew shāchāh (H7812) — to bow down, worship (the OT cousin verb; the LXX often translates with proskuneō).

Usage

"Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve—Christ’s answer to Satan’s third temptation sets the exclusivity standard."

"Peter and the angel refuse proskuneō; Christ accepts it—the Christological inference is unmistakable: the One who accepts what creatures must refuse is God."

"Disembodied contemporary worship loses the body the verb physically names; idolatrous direction toward creatures violates the First Commandment; biblical proskuneō is embodied, in spirit and in truth, to God alone."
